questions.prompt: What is the chapter's core definition of process power?
choices: A company becomes very efficient and disciplined over time
A deeply embedded set of interlocking activities yields lower cost or better product and rivals need prolonged commitment to match it
A company owns a scarce input that rivals cannot buy

explanation.gentle: The chapter requires an interlocking system plus a hard replication burden, not just general efficiency.
explanation.direct: Process power exists when the coordinated machine, not one routine, creates the advantage.
explanation.competitive: No welded system, no process moat.

questions.prompt: Why do interlocking activities matter in this chapter?
choices: Because they help a company look more organized to outsiders
Because the benefit comes from how routines reinforce one another rather than from one isolated move
Because regulators require process documentation

explanation.gentle: The chapter's benefit comes from coordinated links among activities.
explanation.direct: Interlocking activities matter because the system, not a single practice, creates the result.
explanation.competitive: The moat lives in the links, not in the headline tactic.

questions.prompt: Which case best shows ordinary operational excellence rather than process power?
choices: A firm has one efficient routine, but copying it would erase most of the advantage
A rival needs years to rebuild many linked routines that support lower cost
A company has an embedded system whose visible routines underperform when copied outside the full structure

explanation.gentle: If copying one routine removes most of the edge, the system moat is probably weak.
explanation.direct: The first option lacks the deeper interlocking structure that the chapter requires.
explanation.competitive: One good move is not the same as a buried machine.

questions.prompt: Maya sees a rival copying one visible workflow tactic. What should she test before assuming the moat is gone?
choices: Whether the copied move depended on a larger reinforcing system that the rival has not rebuilt
Whether the rival used similar colors and labels
Whether the copied tactic is easier to explain in a presentation

explanation.gentle: The visible move may have drawn strength from hidden linked routines.
explanation.direct: Maya should check whether the copied tactic still lacks the surrounding system that made it powerful.
explanation.competitive: The rival may have stolen the storefront and missed the engine.

questions.prompt: Priya's capstone team uses a board that other teams can copy, but the real speed seems to come from linked review and handoff habits. What does that suggest?
choices: The board alone is the full source of process power
The visible tool is only one piece of a larger interlocking system
The team really has cornered-resource power

explanation.gentle: The board matters, but the linked routines around it appear to carry the deeper advantage.
explanation.direct: This fits the chapter's warning that one visible practice is not the whole moat.
explanation.competitive: The sticky notes are not the machine.

questions.prompt: A student organization copies one tactic from a stronger peer group and still fails to match results. What is the strongest explanation?
choices: The tactic was illegal to copy correctly
The original advantage depended on reinforcing routines that were not reproduced
The stronger group actually had branding power instead

explanation.gentle: The visible tactic probably depended on a deeper system of linked activities.
explanation.direct: The failure suggests the copycat missed the interlocking routines that carried the original result.
explanation.competitive: They stole the move and left the machinery behind.

questions.prompt: Lena notices a local service's quality comes from many small linked routines rather than one trick. What changed in her understanding?
choices: She shifted from seeing a tactic to seeing a reinforcing process
She discovered the service had switching costs
She realized the service had a cornered resource

explanation.gentle: She now sees the result as a system effect rather than as a single clever move.
explanation.direct: The linked habits reveal process logic instead of isolated operational flair.
explanation.competitive: She stopped praising the trick and found the machine.

questions.prompt: Why does prolonged commitment matter so much in this chapter?
choices: Because rivals must rebuild many reinforcing routines coherently over time
Because long meetings improve organizational memory
Because customers prefer firms with older procedures

explanation.gentle: One copied move is easy, but rebuilding the whole supporting system is not.
explanation.direct: Process power is protected because replication requires sustained work across many linked activities.
explanation.competitive: The rival is rebuilding a machine, not photocopying a memo.

questions.prompt: What would most weaken a claim of process power?
choices: The advantage disappears as soon as one visible routine is copied
The process includes many handoffs and standards
The operation produces lower cost and better output together

explanation.gentle: A real process moat should survive surface imitation better than that.
explanation.direct: If copying one visible move erases the edge, the deeper interlocking barrier was probably overstated.
explanation.competitive: If the shiny routine was the whole moat, there was no buried machine.

questions.prompt: This chapter closes strategy statics with an embedded operating system moat. What would signal the next chapter's focus instead?
choices: How firms build power through dynamics rather than merely describing existing power
How customers pay a premium because of brand trust
How scarce inputs create hard-to-match access

explanation.gentle: The next chapter moves from what existing power looks like to how power gets built.
explanation.direct: The book shifts from statics to dynamics by focusing on the path to power.
explanation.competitive: Next, the question stops being 'what is the moat' and becomes 'how do you build one'.
